result.summary: Pausanias describes dedications and statues on the Athenian Acropolis, including the Erechtheum's relics, the rite of the two carrier maidens, and a statue of Tolmides. He then recounts legends of Theseus shown in bronze: the lion's skin at Troezen, the lifting of the stone, and the Marathonian bull.

scenes.title: Relics in Athene's temple
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists old offerings, Persian spoils, the olive and the temple of Pandrosus, doubting the Persian trophies' provenance.

scenes.title: The carrier maidens' night rite
scenes.summary: Two maidens carry unknown objects down an underground passage to a sanctuary of Aphrodite, swap them for others, and are replaced.

place.name: Enclosure of Aphrodite of the Gardens

scenes.title: Statues and Tolmides
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes statues of Lysimache, Erechtheus and Eumolpus, Tolmides' campaigns and death, old Athene statues scorched by Xerxes, and reliefs of hunts and fights.
scenes.stakes: Tolmides' campaign ends in his death and the loss of his army at Haliartia.

scenes.title: Young Theseus at Troezen
scenes.summary: Theseus, aged seven, faces Hercules' lion skin unafraid, and at eighteen lifts the stone to retrieve Ægeus' tokens.

scenes.title: The bull and the Minotaur tribute
scenes.summary: The bull sent by Poseidon ravages Crete and Attica, kills Androgeos, leads to Minos' tribute demand, and is finally sacrificed by Theseus.
scenes.stakes: Athens must send seven youths and seven maidens to the Minotaur.

alias_notes.explanation: Polias means 'of the city', her title as Athens' protectress.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid anecdote of the child Theseus's fearlessness before Hercules' lion skin.

analysis.text: Pausanias mixes sightseeing with critical doubt, questioning how Persian trophies were acquired and misnamed statues.
The passage shows Athens' civic memory: Persian War relics, mythic origins, and Theseus as national hero shaped the Acropolis.

fun_facts.text: The olive's regrowth of two cubits in a day after the Persian burning echoes Herodotus' account of the same miracle.

language_notes.text: A scimetar is a curved single-edged sword of Eastern type; Pausanias reports it only as 'said to have belonged' to Mardonius.
Alludes to the contest of Athene and Poseidon for Attica, in which her gift of the olive won her the land.
A cubit is an ancient measure of about the forearm's length, roughly 18 inches (45 cm).
Refers to the myth of Cecrops' daughters, who were forbidden to open the chest containing the child Erichthonius; Pandrosus alone obeyed.
The maidens' Greek title is usually rendered Arrephoroi; here translated as 'carriers of the holy things'.
A cubit is an ancient measure of roughly a forearm's length, about 18 inches, so the statue is quite small.
Pausanias points out that the pairing is odd: in Athenian tradition Erechtheus killed Immaradus, Eumolpus' son, not Eumolpus himself, so the identification may be wrong.
Xerxes, king of Persia, captured and burnt Athens in 480 BC after the Athenians evacuated to their ships.
The Calydonian boar was a monstrous beast sent by Artemis to ravage Calydon and hunted by heroes.
"Helter skelter" means in confused, headlong flight; it is the translator's colloquial rendering.
"Boots" here means sandals or shoes, left with the sword as tokens by which Ægeus could recognise his son.
"Covenanted" means agreed by treaty; the Athenians accepted the tribute terms.

context_notes.text: Athene Polias, 'Athene of the City', was the Acropolis's chief protector goddess; her old temple housed the most ancient cult objects.
Mardonius, Persian commander, died at Plataea in 479 BC; Masistius, his cavalry chief, fell in a skirmish before the battle.
Aphrodite of the Gardens had a precinct near the Acropolis's slopes; the rite's secret objects remained unknown even to the participants.
Tolmides led an Athenian fleet around the Peloponnese in about 456 BC during the conflict with Sparta.
Tolmides was killed at Coronea in 447 BC, a defeat that ended Athenian control of Bœotia.
Pittheus was king of Troezen and grandfather of Theseus, whose mother Æthra was his daughter.
Poseidon was god of the sea. Minos' sea power made his neglect of the god a notable slight.
The Minotaur was a half-man, half-bull monster kept in the Labyrinth; Theseus later killed it.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias critically weighs the claim, using logic about who killed whom to doubt the relic's authenticity, showing his skeptical narrative voice.
The olive burnt yet sprouting two cubits in a day symbolizes Athens' resilience after the Persian destruction.
Pausanias speaks personally, promising rarer lore and presenting himself as a curious traveller rather than a mere catalogue-maker.
The boy attacks a mere skin as if it were alive, a comic image foreshadowing his later monster-slaying courage.
Pausanias shows his rationalizing, antiquarian voice by sorting the ancient monsters into origins: born of the earth, sacred to gods, or sent as punishment.
